title: Eagles Consider Short‑Term IR for Jalen Hurts After Blood Clot Diagnosis – NBC Sports Report
body:
Philadelphia’s quarterback juggernaut Jalen Hur‑Hurts is once again at the center of the Eagles’ roster puzzle as the organization weighs a short‑term placement on injured reserve (IR) following the discovery of a blood‑clotting issue. The decision, expected to be made on Saturday, could determine whether the 26‑year‑old stays on the sidelines for a few weeks or returns sooner than the league’s standard eight‑week IR minimum. The move would be a strategic gamble for a team that is perched near the top of the NFC East and still vying for a deep playoff run.

Hur‑Hurts, who has been the driving force behind Philadelphia’s resurgence this season, missed two games in early October after a routine scan revealed a clot in his lower leg. He returned to action with a strong performance against the New York Giants, throwing for 271 yards and rushing for 85, helping the Eagles secure a 31‑13 victory. However, team physicians have continued to monitor the clot, and the risk of recurrence remains a concern. A short‑term IR designation would allow the team to retain Hur‑Hurts on the 53‑man roster while freeing a spot for a backup quarterback or a versatile depth player, without committing to the full eight‑week absence that a standard IR placement would entail.

The Eagles’ medical staff, led by head team physician Dr. Greg Gattuso, has reportedly been in close contact with both the NFL’s health‑policy officials and the league’s concussion and cardiovascular experts. The consensus among the doctors is that Hur‑Hurts is medically cleared to play, but the clot’s nature—whether it is a superficial thrombosis that can be managed with anticoagulants or a deeper venous issue—has yet to be fully disclosed. “We are taking a cautious approach,” a team spokesperson said, “because the health of our player is paramount, and we want to ensure there’s no lingering risk for him or his teammates.”

If the Eagles opt for a short‑term IR move, they would be among a small group of teams to use the relatively new rule that permits a player to return after as few as three weeks, provided they are cleared by the league’s medical board. This flexibility was introduced in 2023 to accommodate injuries that do not necessitate a full season‑long recovery period, such as minor soft‑tissue issues or, in rare cases, controlled blood‑clot scenarios. The decision could also impact the team’s offensive game plan. Should Hur‑Hurts be sidelined for even a short stretch, backup quarterback Gardner Minshew—who has been on the active roster as the third‑string option—may see increased snaps, while the Eagles could lean more heavily on their dynamic running backs, especially Miles Sanders and Kenneth Gainwell, to maintain offensive momentum.

Strategically, the move carries implications beyond the immediate roster shuffle. Philadelphia sits at 7‑2, trailing the Dallas Cowboys by a half‑game in the division and holding a tiebreaker edge over the New York Giants. A prolonged absence for Hur‑Hurts could open a window for a rival to close the gap, especially with the Cowboys’ own quarterback situation stabilizing after a strong start. Conversely, a swift return could reinforce the Eagles’ status as a legitimate Super Bowl contender, bolstering their pass‑run balance and keeping their defense off the field longer—a critical factor given the unit’s recent struggles against high‑powered offenses.

The upcoming decision also underscores a broader trend in the NFL: teams are increasingly leveraging medical protocols and roster flexibility to navigate health challenges without sacrificing competitive edge. As the league continues to refine its guidelines around clotting disorders—a concern that has risen in visibility after several high‑profile cases in recent seasons—Philadelphia’s handling of Hur‑Hurts’ situation may set a precedent for how other franchises address similar issues.

Looking ahead, all eyes will be on the Eagles’ front office and medical team as they balance player safety with championship aspirations. If Hur‑Hurts can return after a brief IR stint, Philadelphia’s offense will likely regain its full throttle, keeping the Eagles in the hunt for the NFC East crown and a deep postseason run. Should the clot prove more stubborn, the organization will need to lean on its depth and adapt its play‑calling, testing the resilience of a squad that has already shown it can thrive under adversity. Either scenario promises to shape the narrative of the Eagles’ 2024 campaign in the weeks to come.
